newsitem.title: BELGIUM: France's jobless rise seen clouding EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: France's jobless rise seen clouding EMU debate.

text.p: France's stagnant jobs market and the added uncertainty it creates for government finances have raised doubts over of how much flexibility will be needed in determining who qualifies for EMU, analysts said on Monday.
It has become accepted in most quarters that for the euro to be launched on schedule in 1999 there will have to be a more liberal interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty's deficit criterion.
France has already admitted this and a critical test of what the new Socialist government believes is feasible will come on July 21 when it unveils an audit of its budget.
The only question in the minds of most experts is by how much Paris is prepared to miss the Maastricht Treaty's deficit target of three percent to gross domestic product.

"That will be a critical moment for the government because it will indeed determine the level they will go public with on the deficit," says Paul Horne, chief international economist with Smith Barney in Paris.

If the outcome is at or above 3.5 percent of GDP, analysts say the reaction in Germany, itself struggling to keep the tide of red ink just above the treaty's threshold, could be uncomprimising at best.

This does not mean that economic reality has not begun to dawn on the former paragon of European fiscal correctness. There are growing signs that Bonn, committed to seeing EMU launched on time, will accept a more generous reading of the euro's preconditions.
Even the stern hand of the Bundesbank appears to be wavering slightly on the issue of budgetary rigour.
"The three percent (deficit to GDP ratio set down in the Maastricht Treaty) is an important reference number," said Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Sunday.

"But more important than the one-off fulfilment, or bare undershooting or overshooting of this number, is the question as to whether countries' public finances...are in a condition that can be viewed as sustainable," he added.
In other words, the 1997 budget performance of countries wanting to get into monetary union may be only part of the picture, with 1998 becoming a much more important assessment.

But just how much leeway the EU will have when deciding on the euro's founding members is unclear. Analysts say the two most important factors in this debate are the new political regime in France and the growing row within German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition.

Commenting on France's May jobless rise of 32,400 on Monday -- which left the country's unemployment rate unchanged at 12.5 percent -- some economists were less than sanguine about the political and policy implications.
"From a political standpoint, it is clearly a number that will put pressure on the government to take quick measures," said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris.
"It is the business cycle which will do the job (of reducing unemployment), but there will be big pressure (on the government) to accelerate its jobs policy."

Meanwhile in Germany, the rift between Kohl's CDU and its counterpart, the Christian Socialist Union (CSU), shows no signs of healing, with Bavarian premier and CSU leader Edmund Stoiber continuing a high publicity campaign for strict interpretation of EMU's entry critiera.
Many commentators in Germany believe Stoiber's tactics have much to do with politics and standing up to Kohl ahead of regional state elections next year.
But there are doubts over whether France has a sufficient awareness and understanding of Germany's internal bickering.
"I don't think the French government really recognises that the Kohl government doesn't have much leeway on the deficit," added Horne of Smith Barney.

Just how close the two countries are in appreciating each other's respective political circumstances may hold the key to whether the momentum behind EMU, now a forgone conclusion in financial markets, will remain intact, say analysts.
